title: What Changed Around the Press
framing: This prologue sets 55 of the count's own acts in seven sections: access to the president, the FCC's power over broadcast licenses, public media funding, lawsuits against outlets, the Justice Department's rules on reporters' records, and the government's public data and briefings. It closes with what the courts blocked and what they let stand. Every step comes from an act the count records; the prologue orders them by subject and claims no cause between any two of them.
method: Seven themed finders read the Trump Tracker corpus and the press ledger; a verifier per theme checked every beat against its entry (facts, verbatim sources, dates, quotes and who the entry attributes them to); a synthesis wrote the outline; a critic checked it for completeness and overreach; one gap-fill round followed. Every URL below appears in a tracker entry or the ledger; the gate ran after the sweep with zero misses.

sections.title: Who gets near the president
sections.thesis: Trump's campaigns denied credentials to named outlets in 2016 and 2024, and his first-term press office kept outlets out of a briefing. In the second term the White House took over the press pool and required appointments to enter the press secretary's office, while the Pentagon evicted outlets from their workspaces, required escorts and imposed credential rules that a judge struck in March 2026.

beats.line: In June 2016, the Trump campaign revoked the Washington Post's press credentials, adding it to a list of outlets it had barred, over what Trump called its "incredibly inaccurate coverage and reporting" of his campaign, after objecting to a Post headline on his Orlando shooting remarks.
beats.why: A campaign's credential list excluded outlets by name; NPR listed earlier exclusions including HuffPost, Politico, BuzzFeed, the Daily Beast, the Des Moines Register and Univision.
beats.quote: phony and dishonest

sections.title: The FCC and broadcast licenses
sections.thesis: Trump publicly urged a challenge to NBC's license in 2017 and called for taking away CBS's in 2024. In the second term Chairman Carr's FCC reinstated dismissed complaints against three networks' stations, and Carr warned ABC's affiliates hours before two station groups pulled Kimmel, warned broadcasters about their license renewals during the Iran war and said fake news shows would not qualify for the equal-time exemption. The FCC also ordered early reviews of ABC's licenses and voted to scrap the 39 percent ownership cap.

beats.line: On October 11, 2017, Trump asked when it would be "appropriate to challenge" NBC's license, and the next day said network licenses "must be challenged and if appropriate revoked."
beats.why: A first-term instance of the president publicly urging a challenge to a network's FCC license.

sections.title: Defunding public media and cutting the government's broadcasters
sections.thesis: A first-term budget asked Congress to end public broadcasting funding, and the first-term head of the global media agency fired its networks' chiefs. In the second term Carr opened an underwriting probe of NPR and PBS, and the agency put 1,042 staff on leave and ended two networks' grants. A rescission law canceled the Corporation for Public Broadcasting's funding, while an executive order against NPR and PBS was later permanently blocked, and an inspector general found that the agency's cuts skipped key steps.

sections.title: Suits, settlements and threats
sections.thesis: His campaign's 2020 suits against three outlets were dismissed, ABC paid $15 million to his library to settle a 2024 suit, and as president-elect he said suing the media "should have been the Justice Department or somebody else." In the second term Paramount paid $16 million while its merger awaited FCC approval, which came three weeks later with conditions reaching CBS. The White House dropped the Journal from a pool after he sued it, he sued the BBC for $10 billion, and the White House counsel gave Politico 48 hours to correct or retract three stories.

beats.line: In February 2020, the Trump campaign sued the New York Times, then within ten days the Washington Post and CNN, over 2019 opinion pieces; all three suits were dismissed, the CNN suit for failure to plead actual malice.
beats.why: His campaign sued three outlets in the first term and courts dismissed all three; the CNN dismissal came with leave to amend.

sections.title: Reporters' records and leak hunts
sections.thesis: In the first term, by Comey's account, Trump raised jailing reporters with the FBI director, Sessions announced a review of media subpoena rules, and the department took reporters' phone and email records, which surfaced months later. In June 2021, after the first term, the department said it would stop seizing reporters' records in leak cases. In April 2025 Bondi rescinded what NPR called Biden-era protections, after which the FBI searched a reporter's home, four Times reporters were subpoenaed and DHS obtained a journalist's phone records with a summons that needs no judge.

critic.verdict: The outline mostly holds up. All 16 tracker ids exist in the corpus, and every ledger-keyed beat matches its ledger item. Every quote has a quoteBy that matches the entry's or ledger's attribution, apart from the minor quoteBy notes in overreach. The causation discipline is sound: the Kimmel, Paramount, WSJ pool and Times subpoena beats state sequence only. Of the eight themes, these are covered with real entries: the pool takeover and the AP ban; the FCC's license threats and revived complaints; the defunding of public media and the dismantling of VOA; the rescission of the subpoena rules; the removal of public data and the firing of the BLS commissioner; the CNN, MS NOW and Politico ban and the ruling against it; and the Pentagon pledge. Two themes are only partly covered. The settlements and suits leave out Meta, and the WSJ and BBC suits appear only as references, never as beats. The merger probes leave out the Skydance conditions, Carr's Comcast and Disney DEI probes, the August 2026 vote to end the ownership cap and the Paramount foreign-ownership waiver. The biggest omissions of setup acts are these: Carr's January 2025 underwriting probe of NPR and PBS; USAGM's March 15, 2025 leave and grant terminations; the CPB board firings; the May 2025 Pentagon escort memo; the campaign's 2024 credential denials, which named Politico; Trump's 2023 vows to scrutinize the media and 'come down hard' on MSNBC; the license threats between the terms; and the suits filed between the terms, beyond ABC and CBS. Several of these are not even on the left-out list. Overreach is limited and fixable, and nothing is fabricated. The main fixes are these. The Justice Department thesis places the June 2021 pledge to stop in the wrong administration. The public-media thesis credits a blocked executive order with the funding cut. The access thesis and the Hillyard beat state one reporter's account as fact. The January 22 why calls all three revived complaints news distortion. The ownership-cap line is out of date. The limits section leaves out the appellate rulings that went the government's way. Fix those, add the three or four strongest missing steps (the underwriting probe, the USAGM leave, the 2024 Politico credential denial and the 2023 'come down hard' posts), and the outline meets the template's standard.

The summary on reporters' records says the home search and the subpoenas came after Bondi's rescission. It gives order, not cause.

The summary on public media says the rescission law canceled the Corporation for Public Broadcasting's funding. It does not credit the cut to the executive order against NPR and PBS, which was blocked.

Twenty steps give reasons drawn by inference, not stated in their records. On access and the FCC: the 2017 Spicer briefing, Trump's 2017 NBC license post, the Kimmel affiliates, Carr's equal-time statement and the ownership cap.

On public media and suits: the 2017 budget, Michael Pack's firings, Carr's underwriting probe, the rescission, the 2020 campaign suits, the ABC suit, the Mar-a-Lago remark and the FCC's approval of Skydance's purchase of Paramount.

Nine reasons marked as stated carry a record's own analysis or another party's words rather than a finding: the Iran war license warning, Disney review, BBC suit, DHS summons, data deletions, inspector general, satellite withhold, 2024 credentials and BLS firing.

Some dates mark a report, not the event: press coverage of the inspector general's evaluation, which is dated September 2026; the DHS summons; the satellite withhold, which reaches back to March 9, 2026; and the data deletions.

Other dates fall on one event among several: the rescission (signed July 24, 2025, requested June 3), the Watkins notice, the email-logs order, the NPR and PBS order and the Pentagon appeals stays. Carr's step uses its record's date.
Records disagree on two dates, and the page follows this count’s own: the Pentagon credential ruling, March 20, 2026 (another says March 21); Friedman’s violation finding, April 9 (April 10).

Many quotations are fragments of longer statements. On access and the FCC: Trump's 'phony and dishonest', Tara Palmeri, the Pentagon Press Association, the Upper Press memo, which starts mid-sentence, Trump's 2017 license post, Rosenworcel and Gomez on the ownership cap.

Also fragments: Carr on the Paramount talks, said April 28, 2025, before the settlement; Comey's memo; Sessions; Bondi's memo; the Justice Department on the Times subpoenas; the HHS memo; the CDC records quotation; Planet Labs; and Judge Lamberth.

Trump's words in the step on finding leakers come from Comey's memo, which is Comey's account of the meeting. Tara Palmeri's reason for her credential denial is her own account.

The Office of Special Counsel's finding of a 'substantial likelihood of wrongdoing' was against the global media agency, not specifically against Michael Pack's firings.
No company or official has said the FCC's approval of the Paramount merger depended on the settlement.

Still in court: the ruling on CNN's, MS NOW's and Politico's White House passes is a preliminary injunction under appeal; the AP's appeal is undecided; ABC's suit over its license review had no ruling as of October 8, 2026.
